title: Text as Bytes: ASCII, UTF-8, and Unicode
summary: See the bytes behind every string: ASCII, UTF-8's variable width, counting and decoding code points, feed pitfalls, and std::regex.
intro: A reference file from a European exchange lists `Nestlé` and `Zürich Insurance`, and three steps of your loader break at once: a length check rejects the names, the uppercase step skips letters, and the first column header never matches. All three bugs have one cause. A `std::string` holds bytes, and text is an agreement about what those bytes mean. This lesson covers ASCII, Unicode and UTF-8, why `size()` counts bytes, decoding code points, the traps real feeds bring, and matching patterns with `std::regex`.

steps.title: ASCII and the bytes of a string
steps.body:
*Looping Over Strings*, the last lesson, treated a `char` as a small number, its character code, with `'A'` at 65. Which number stands for which character is fixed by an **encoding**, and the oldest one still everywhere is **ASCII**. It has 128 codes, 0 to 127:

| Codes | Characters |
| --- | --- |
| 0 to 31, and 127 | control codes: `'\0'` is 0, `'\t'` is 9, `'\n'` is 10, `'\r'` is 13 |
| 32 to 126 | printable: space, punctuation, `'0'` to `'9'` at 48 to 57, `'A'` to `'Z'` at 65 to 90, `'a'` to `'z'` at 97 to 122 |

Control codes print as nothing, or move the cursor, so they hide in output. Two of them bite in trading code. The FIX protocol separates the fields of an order with SOH, code 1, so a raw message in a log looks like one long word. And a file saved on Windows ends each line with `"\r\n"`, so a line read on Linux or a Mac can end in an invisible `'\r'`, and `"AAPL\r" == "AAPL"` is false.

To see what's really there, print each byte in hex, two digits from `00` to `FF`, as *Numbers in Memory: Binary, Two's Complement, and IEEE 754* did. A `\x` escape puts a byte into a literal by its hex value: `'\x01'` is SOH.

```cpp
const std::string s = "35=D\x01";
for (char c : s) {
    const int code = static_cast<unsigned char>(c);
    std::cout << std::hex << std::uppercase << std::setw(2) << std::setfill('0') << code << ' ';
}
std::cout << std::dec << '\n';  // 33 35 3D 44 01
```

`std::hex` and `std::dec` work as they did there, `std::uppercase` prints `3D` rather than `3d`, and `std::setw(2)` with `std::setfill('0')` keeps `01` from shrinking to `1`. The byte goes into an `int` so that `<<` prints a number, not the character, and through `unsigned char` on the way. Plain `char` is signed here, so a byte above 127 would become a negative `int` and print as `FFFFFFE2`.

> Gotcha: a `\x` escape takes every hex digit that follows it. `"\x0155=AAPL"` isn't SOH then `55`. g++ warns `hex escape sequence out of range` and keeps one wrong byte, and clang on your Mac stops with that error. Split the literal instead: `"\x01" "55=AAPL"`, since side-by-side literals join into one, as *From Source to Executable: Preprocess, Compile, Link* showed.

example.title: FIX bytes made visible
example.prompt: Count the fields of a FIX message by its SOH separators, print the first field's bytes in hex, and build a readable copy with | in place of SOH.
example.output:
bytes: 30
fields: 4
hex of field 1: 38 3D 46 49 58 2E 34 2E 32 01
readable: 8=FIX.4.2|35=D|55=AAPL|38=100|
example.explanation:
`SOH` is the char with code 1. Joining it with `+` needs a `std::string` on one side, which is why the message starts with `std::string("8=FIX.4.2")`. The 30 bytes hold 4 SOH bytes, so there are 4 fields.

The hex loop runs from index 0 through the first SOH, which `find` reports at index 9. Each byte goes through `unsigned char` into an `int`, and `std::setw(2)` with `std::setfill('0')` pads it to two digits, so SOH shows as `01`. `std::dec` after the loop puts the stream back to base 10 for the lines that follow.

The last loop copies every byte and swaps SOH for `|`, the separator later lessons write when they show FIX messages.

practice.title: A Windows line ending
practice.prompt:
Find and remove the hidden `'\r'` at the end of a line from a Windows file.

1. After `hex:`, print a space and then each byte of `line` as two uppercase hex digits.
2. Set `endsWithCr` to true when `line` isn't empty and its last byte is `'\r'`.
3. When it is, remove that byte with `pop_back`.
4. Keep the starter's other lines, which print the sizes and compare the price.

Expected output:

```text
bytes: 12
hex: 4D 53 46 54 2C 34 31 30 2E 32 35 0D
ends with CR: true
cleaned bytes: 11
price is 410.25: true
```

tests.output:
bytes: 12
hex: 4D 53 46 54 2C 34 31 30 2E 32 35 0D
ends with CR: true
cleaned bytes: 11
price is 410.25: true

hints: Copy the example's hex loop, with a range-for over `line` in place of the index loop.
`'\r'` is code 13, which prints as `0D`. Check it with `line.back() == '\r'`.

steps.title: Unicode and UTF-8

example.title: Bytes, code points, and padding
example.prompt: For each name, count its bytes and code points, and pad it to 8 code points so the columns line up.
example.output:
AAPL    | 4 bytes, 4 code points
Zürich  | 7 bytes, 6 code points
€100    | 6 bytes, 4 code points
Nestlé  | 7 bytes, 6 code points
Ελλάδα  | 12 bytes, 6 code points
example.explanation:
`name.size()` counts bytes, so `Zürich` is 7: the `ü` is the two bytes `C3 BC`. The inner loop counts one code point per byte that starts a character, a byte below `0x80` (ASCII) or from `0xC0` up (a lead byte), and skips the continuation bytes from `0x80` to `0xBF`. `€` is three bytes and one code point, so `€100` has 6 bytes and 4 code points, and each Greek letter of `Ελλάδα` takes 2 bytes.

`std::string(8 - points, ' ')` pads by code points, so every `|` lands in the same column on screen. Every name here shows one column per code point. A wide character like `日` would need a display width count, which the C++17 library doesn't have.

practice.title: A column of company names
practice.prompt:
Print a table of names padded by code points, and count the names that are pure ASCII.

1. Count the code points of each name with the continuation byte test.
2. Print the name, spaces up to 9 code points, `| `, its bytes, and its code points, as shown.
3. Count the names whose byte count equals their code point count, and keep the starter's last line.

Expected output:

```text
BMW      | 3 bytes, 3 code points
Société  | 9 bytes, 7 code points
¥500     | 5 bytes, 4 code points
Δέλτα    | 10 bytes, 5 code points
Ørsted   | 7 bytes, 6 code points
ASCII only: 1
```

tests.output:
BMW      | 3 bytes, 3 code points
Société  | 9 bytes, 7 code points
¥500     | 5 bytes, 4 code points
Δέλτα    | 10 bytes, 5 code points
Ørsted   | 7 bytes, 6 code points
ASCII only: 1

hints: The example's inner loop works unchanged. Pad with `std::string(9 - points, ' ')`.
`name.size()` is a `std::size_t`, so compare it as `static_cast<int>(name.size()) == points`.

steps.title: Decoding code points safely
steps.body:
Sometimes you need the code point itself, say to check that a name uses only Latin letters. A lead byte says how long the character is and carries its first bits, and each continuation byte adds 6 more. The usual tools are the shifts and masks of *Bitwise Operations*, later in the course, but plain arithmetic works too: subtract each byte's marker, then multiply by 64 (that's 2^6) for every continuation byte after it. The markers are `0xC0` for a 2-byte lead, `0xE0` for 3, `0xF0` for 4, and `0x80` for continuation bytes.

```cpp
const int b0 = 0xE2, b1 = 0x82, b2 = 0xAC;  // the bytes of €
const int point = ((b0 - 0xE0) * 64 + (b1 - 0x80)) * 64 + (b2 - 0x80);
std::cout << std::hex << std::uppercase << point << '\n';  // 20AC
```

Byte-level code breaks UTF-8 in quieter ways too. All of these come up in real reference data:

- **Cutting at a byte count.** A fixed-width column can end inside a character, and the half character shows as �. Before you cut at byte `n`, move `n` back while `s[n]` is a continuation byte.
- **`<cctype>` sees bytes.** `std::toupper` leaves both bytes of `é` alone, so an uppercase loop turns `Nestlé` into `NESTLé`. Real case mapping needs a Unicode library such as ICU.
- **Reversing bytes** scrambles every character longer than one byte.
- **A byte order mark.** Excel may start a UTF-8 file with `EF BB BF`, so the first header is `"\xEF\xBB\xBFsymbol"`, not `"symbol"`. Erase those 3 bytes when a file starts with them.
- **Look-alikes.** `é` can be one code point, U+00E9, or `e` plus a combining accent, U+0301. They look the same and compare unequal.
- **The wrong encoding.** UTF-8 read as Windows-1252 turns `é` into `Ã©`, which is called mojibake.

C++ has wider character types. `char32_t` holds one code point, `U"€"` is a `char32_t` literal, and `std::u32string` keeps one element per code point. `wchar_t` is 4 bytes on Linux and macOS but 2 on Windows, so portable code avoids it, and most code keeps UTF-8 in `std::string`. C++20 adds `char8_t` and changes `u8"Zürich"` from plain `char` text into it, which breaks code like this on your Mac's clang:

```text
$ clang++ -std=c++20 u8.cpp -o u8
u8.cpp:5:17: error: no viable conversion from 'const char8_t[8]' to 'std::string' (aka 'basic_string<char>')
    5 |     std::string city = u8"Zürich";
```

example.title: Code points and a safe cut
example.prompt: Decode a string into its code points, then cut a company name to fit an 8-byte column without splitting a character.
example.output:
U+005A in 1 byte(s)
U+00E9 in 2 byte(s)
U+20AC in 3 byte(s)
U+1F680 in 4 byte(s)
cut at 7: Sociét
example.explanation:
The lead byte picks the length. `é` starts with `0xC3`, so it's 2 bytes, and `point` starts as `0xC3 - 0xC0`, which is 3. The continuation byte `0xA9` is worth `0xA9 - 0x80`, which is 41, so `point` becomes `3 * 64 + 41`, which is 233, or `0xE9`. 🚀 takes all four bytes, and its code point needs five hex digits, which `std::setw(4)` allows since it's a minimum width. `i += length` jumps to the next lead byte.

In `Société Générale`, bytes 7 and 8 are the second `é`. Byte 8 is its continuation byte, so the loop moves `cut` back to 7, where the `é` starts, and `substr(0, 7)` keeps `Sociét`. Cutting at 8 would have kept half of the `é`.

practice.title: Currency signs and a short column
practice.prompt:
Decode a string of currency signs, then cut a name to a 6-byte column safely.

1. In the decode loop, set `length` and `point` from the lead byte as the example does, for 2, 3, and 4 byte characters.
2. Add each continuation byte with `point = point * 64 + (byte - 0x80)`.
3. Move `cut` back while `name[cut]` is a continuation byte, then keep the starter's print.

Expected output:

```text
U+0041 in 1 byte(s)
U+00A3 in 2 byte(s)
U+20AC in 3 byte(s)
U+1F4B6 in 4 byte(s)
cut at 5: Nestl
```

tests.output:
U+0041 in 1 byte(s)
U+00A3 in 2 byte(s)
U+20AC in 3 byte(s)
U+1F4B6 in 4 byte(s)
cut at 5: Nestl

hints: Test the largest marker first: `lead >= 0xF0`, then `0xE0`, then `0xC0`.
In `Nestlé SA`, byte 5 starts the `é` and byte 6 is its continuation byte, so the cut lands at 5.

steps.title: Matching patterns with std::regex
steps.body:
Reference data needs checking before a strategy trusts it. Is `BRK.B` a valid symbol? What are the symbol, quantity, and price in a fill line from a log? A **regular expression** describes a pattern of text in a small language of its own:

| Pattern | Matches |
| --- | --- |
| `[A-Z]`, `[A-Z0-9]` | one char from the set |
| `\d` | one digit |
| `x{1,5}`, `x+`, `x?` | 1 to 5 of `x`, 1 or more, 0 or 1 |
| `\.` | a dot, since a bare `.` matches any char |
| `( )` | a capture group, saved for you to read |

`<regex>` brings them to C++. `std::regex` holds a compiled pattern. `std::regex_match(s, re)` is true when all of `s` matches. `std::regex_search(s, m, re)` finds the first match anywhere in `s` and fills `m`, a `std::smatch`: `m[0]` is the whole match, `m[1]` the first group, and `m.str(1)` gives it as a `std::string`. Write patterns as raw strings, so each backslash stays a single one.

```cpp
const std::regex qty(R"(qty=(\d+))");
const std::string order = "NEW AAPL qty=300 px=192.75";
std::smatch m;
if (std::regex_search(order, m, qty)) {
    std::cout << m[1] << '\n';  // 300
}
```

Patterns see bytes too. A `.` matches one byte, and `[A-Z]` never matches `É`.

Trading code keeps `std::regex` off its hot path, the code that runs for every message. Building a regex parses the pattern and allocates memory, and matching runs a general engine that tries alternatives and backs up. In the sandbox at its default `-O0`, checking 100,000 symbols took about 130 ms with `regex_match` and about 4 ms with a hand-written loop over the chars. With `-O2` it was about 13 ms against 0.25 ms. Building the regex inside the loop added about 190 microseconds per symbol. These are rough times from the emulated sandbox, and libc++'s `std::regex` on your Mac was slower still.

A feed handler has a few microseconds per message. So it builds each pattern once, uses `std::regex` for config files and tests, and parses messages by hand, as the advanced lesson *`string_view` and Fast Parsing* does. Faster engines exist, such as Google's RE2 and the compile-time CTRE.

example.title: Symbols and a fill line
example.prompt: Validate symbols with regex_match, then pull the symbol, quantity, and price out of a log line with regex_search and capture groups.
example.output:
AAPL valid: true
BRK.B valid: true
msft valid: false
GOOGLE valid: false
ÉDF valid: false
match: FILL AAPL 100 @ 192.75
symbol: AAPL, qty: 100, price: 192.75
whole line matches: false
example.explanation:
`[A-Z]{1,5}(\.[A-Z])?` means 1 to 5 capitals, then optionally a dot and one more capital. `regex_match` needs the whole string to fit, so `msft` fails on lowercase and `GOOGLE` on its sixth letter. `ÉDF` fails because `É` is the two bytes `C3 89`, and neither is a capital A to Z.

`regex_search` finds the fill inside the longer line. Its three groups hold `AAPL`, `100`, and `192.75`. `m.str(2)` gives a `std::string` that `std::stoi` can parse, while `m[1]` prints directly. The same pattern fails `regex_match` against the whole line, because the timestamp and venue aren't part of it. Both regexes are built once, before they're used.

practice.title: ISINs and a quote line
practice.prompt:
Validate ISINs, the 12-character codes that identify securities, and parse a quote from a log line.

1. Build `isinPattern`: 2 capital letters, then 9 capitals or digits, then 1 digit.
2. Print each ISIN with `regex_match` against it.
3. Search `line` with a pattern whose 3 groups capture the symbol after `QUOTE `, the price after `bid=`, and the price after `ask=`.
4. Print `symbol: `, then `bid: ` and ` ask: `, then `spread: ` as ask minus bid with 2 decimals.

Expected output:

```text
US0378331005 valid: true
us0378331005 valid: false
US037833100 valid: false
DE000BAY0017 valid: true
symbol: MSFT
bid: 410.20 ask: 410.30
spread: 0.10
```

tests.output:
US0378331005 valid: true
us0378331005 valid: false
US037833100 valid: false
DE000BAY0017 valid: true
symbol: MSFT
bid: 410.20 ask: 410.30
spread: 0.10

hints: Model the quote pattern on the example's fill pattern: `QUOTE ([A-Z.]+) bid=(\d+\.\d+) ask=(\d+\.\d+)`.
Parse the groups with `std::stod(m.str(3))`, and print with `std::fixed << std::setprecision(2)`.

recap:
- A string is bytes. ASCII gives codes 0 to 127, and control codes like SOH (1) and `'\r'` (13) hide in output, so print bytes in hex to see them.
- Print a byte with `static_cast<unsigned char>` first, then `std::hex`, `std::setw(2)`, and `std::setfill('0')`, and switch back with `std::dec`.
- Unicode numbers every character with a code point, and UTF-8 stores it in 1 to 4 bytes. ASCII is valid UTF-8, and continuation bytes are `0x80` to `0xBF`.
- `size()` counts bytes. Count code points by skipping continuation bytes, and pad columns by code points, not with `std::setw`.
- Decode with the lead byte's marker and `* 64` per continuation byte. Cut only where a character starts.
- `<cctype>`, reversing, and byte cuts all break UTF-8. Watch for byte order marks, look-alike characters, and the wrong encoding.
- `std::regex_match` checks a whole string, and `std::regex_search` with `std::smatch` finds a match and its groups.
- `std::regex` is slow. Build it once and keep it off the hot path, where hand-written parsing wins.

That ends the Strings section. Next, **Functions** opens Functions and Building Programs with the first tool for organizing code: naming a piece of work and calling it.
